notes: V5 Stage 3 (Issue #16) atomic claim registry. Each claim is the smallest independently assessable factual proposition supported by content/sources/registry.json — never a bundled paragraph of assertions. This is a small, real seed set (11 claims) spanning the requested domains, intended to exercise the architecture (claim-source contract, trust-tier gating, statistical/trial detail preservation, decay scheduling), not to pre-populate the corpus. Issue #17 will grow this registry as real article research occurs.

claims.canonical_claim: BMI is a surrogate measure of body fatness, not a direct measurement of body fat.
claims.outcome: BMI cannot distinguish fat mass from lean mass
limitations: Does not itself quantify how large the BMI-vs-body-fat discrepancy is for any individual.
allowed_wording: BMI is a surrogate, population-level measure of body fatness
BMI does not directly measure body fat
prohibited_wording: BMI is an accurate measure of body fat for every individual
BMI directly measures body fat
claims.notes: Foundational definitional claim used to qualify any BMI-based statement elsewhere in the corpus.

claims.canonical_claim: During a sufficiently long fasting period, the body shifts from primarily glucose-based to primarily ketone-based fuel use — a shift commonly described as the 'metabolic switch.'
claims.support_strength: single peer-reviewed narrative review (Tier B) synthesizing multiple primary studies
limitations: A narrative review synthesizing many underlying studies, not a single controlled trial of the mechanism itself.
Exact fasting duration needed to trigger the switch varies by individual and was not reduced to one number in this source.
required_qualifiers: timeframe and individual variation in when the switch occurs are not precisely defined by this source
prohibited_wording: the metabolic switch happens at exactly the same time for everyone
fasting immediately switches the body to ketone use
claims.notes: Definitional/mechanistic claim only — not an efficacy or outcome claim about fasting for weight loss. Reverified during the Stage 3 closure pass (Issue #28) against the source's two published NEJM errata (see src-decabo-mattson-2019.corrections[]): neither correction touches anything this claim asserts, since this claim states no specific ketone concentration or hour threshold and makes no adiposity/lifespan claim.

claims.canonical_claim: In the STEP 1 trial, once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg produced a mean body-weight change of -14.9% at week 68, compared with -2.4% for placebo, in adults with overweight or obesity without diabetes.
claims.support_strength: single large phase 3 randomized controlled trial (Tier A)
claims.population: adults with BMI >=30, or >=27 with at least one weight-related comorbidity, without diabetes
claims.intervention_or_exposure: once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg plus lifestyle intervention
claims.outcome: percent change in body weight from baseline to week 68
claims.jurisdiction: multinational clinical trial; result underlies FDA approval in the United States
limitations: Trial population excluded people with diabetes.
68-week result only; does not by itself establish durability beyond the study period.
confounders: Concurrent lifestyle/behavioral intervention was provided to both arms.
allowed_wording: produced a mean body-weight reduction of approximately 15% at 68 weeks in the STEP 1 trial
resulted in significantly greater weight loss than placebo in the STEP 1 trial
required_qualifiers: specific to the STEP 1 trial population (adults without diabetes)
result measured at week 68; not a claim about outcomes at other time points
prohibited_wording: cures obesity
guarantees weight loss
produces the same result for every person
claims.medical_advice_boundary: Describes a clinical trial result; does not constitute a personalized recommendation to use semaglutide.

statistical_detail.measure_type: mean percent change in body weight from baseline
statistical_detail.population: adults with overweight or obesity without diabetes, STEP 1 trial (N=1,961)
statistical_detail.confidence_interval: treatment difference vs placebo: -12.4 percentage points (95% CI -13.4 to -11.5, P<0.001)

trial_detail.population: adults with BMI >=30, or >=27 with a weight-related comorbidity, without diabetes
trial_detail.intervention: once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg plus lifestyle intervention
trial_detail.primary_endpoint: percent change in body weight and proportion achieving >=5% weight loss from baseline to week 68
trial_detail.result: -14.9% mean weight change vs -2.4% placebo; 86.4% vs 31.5% achieved >=5% weight loss
trial_detail.regulatory_relationship: pivotal trial supporting FDA approval of Wegovy (semaglutide 2.4 mg) for chronic weight management

claims.canonical_claim: Wegovy (semaglutide) carries an FDA boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors observed in rodent studies, and is contraindicated in people with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).
claims.outcome: boxed warning + absolute contraindication as stated in labeling
limitations: The thyroid C-cell tumor finding is from rodent studies; the label states human relevance has not been determined.

The current label also lists a separate hypersensitivity contraindication (prior serious hypersensitivity reaction to semaglutide or WEGOVY excipients), which is out of scope for this specific thyroid/MTC/MEN2 claim.
required_qualifiers: applies specifically to Wegovy (semaglutide) FDA-approved prescribing information
thyroid C-cell tumor finding is from rodent studies; human relevance undetermined per the label
allowed_wording: carries a boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors seen in rodent studies
is contraindicated in people with a personal or family history of MTC or MEN 2
prohibited_wording: has been proven to cause thyroid cancer in humans
is safe for everyone regardless of thyroid history
claims.medical_advice_boundary: States what the FDA label discloses; does not substitute for an individualized prescribing decision by a clinician.
claims.notes: Reverified during the Stage 3 closure pass (Issue #28) against the current 2026 Novo Nordisk label (src-fda-wegovy-label, DailyMed setid ee06186f...) after that source replaced a retired 2024 repackaged listing. The boxed warning and MTC/MEN2 contraindication text are confirmed unchanged between the 2024 and 2026 labels, and identical across the injection and tablet formulations — no wording change to this claim was required.

claims.canonical_claim: Wegovy (semaglutide) — in both its original once-weekly subcutaneous injection formulation and its newer oral tablet formulation — is FDA-approved for weight reduction and maintenance in adults with obesity, or with overweight plus at least one weight-related comorbidity, as an adjunct to a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity, and for reducing the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in adults with established cardiovascular disease who have obesity or overweight.
limitations: This claim covers only the adult weight-management and cardiovascular-risk-reduction indications shared by both formulations. It does NOT cover two additional, injection-only indications also present in the current label: weight reduction in pediatric patients aged 12 and older with obesity, and treatment of noncirrhotic MASH (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis) with moderate-to-advanced liver fibrosis in adults. Neither the pediatric nor the MASH indication applies to the tablet formulation per this same label.
required_qualifiers: reflects United States FDA approval status only; regulatory status may differ in other jurisdictions
does not by itself describe the injection-only pediatric-obesity or MASH-treatment indications — those require a separate, dedicated claim if an article needs to state them
prohibited_wording: approved for cosmetic weight loss with no medical indication required
approved for pediatric use or MASH treatment in tablet form
claims.notes: Rewritten during the Stage 3 closure pass (Issue #28): the prior wording named a specific injection dose ("semaglutide 2.4 mg") and did not account for the current label's oral tablet formulation or its two additional injection-only indications (pediatric obesity ages 12+, and MASH treatment) added since the 2024 label this claim originally cited. The dose figure was removed from this claim's scope (a specific dose can differ by formulation and is better carried on a dosing-specific claim if one is added later) and the claim is now explicitly scoped to only the indications the two formulations share.

claims.canonical_claim: In the SURMOUNT-1 trial, once-weekly subcutaneous tirzepatide 15 mg produced a mean body-weight change of -20.9% at week 72, compared with -3.1% for placebo, in adults with obesity or overweight without diabetes.
claims.support_strength: single large phase 3 randomized controlled trial (Tier A)
claims.population: adults with BMI >=30, or >=27 with a weight-related comorbidity, without diabetes
claims.intervention_or_exposure: once-weekly subcutaneous tirzepatide 15 mg plus lifestyle intervention
claims.outcome: percent change in body weight from baseline to week 72
claims.jurisdiction: multinational clinical trial; result underlies FDA approval in the United States
limitations: Trial population excluded people with diabetes.
72-week result only; does not by itself establish durability beyond the study period.
confounders: Concurrent lifestyle/behavioral intervention was provided to both arms.
allowed_wording: produced a mean body-weight reduction of approximately 21% at 72 weeks (15 mg dose) in the SURMOUNT-1 trial
resulted in significantly greater weight loss than placebo across all three tested doses
required_qualifiers: specific to the SURMOUNT-1 trial population (adults without diabetes)
result varies by dose (5/10/15 mg); citing one dose's figure without the dose is misleading
prohibited_wording: cures obesity
guarantees weight loss
produces the same result for every person
claims.medical_advice_boundary: Describes a clinical trial result; does not constitute a personalized recommendation to use tirzepatide.

statistical_detail.measure_type: mean percent change in body weight from baseline
statistical_detail.population: adults with obesity or overweight without diabetes, SURMOUNT-1 trial (N=2,539)
statistical_detail.confidence_interval: placebo-adjusted comparison reported by dose; see primary publication Table 2

trial_detail.population: adults with BMI >=30, or >=27 with a weight-related comorbidity, without diabetes
trial_detail.intervention: once-weekly subcutaneous tirzepatide (5 mg, 10 mg, or 15 mg) plus lifestyle intervention
trial_detail.primary_endpoint: percent change in body weight and proportion achieving >=5% weight loss from baseline to week 72
trial_detail.result: weight change by dose: 5mg -15.0%, 10mg -19.5%, 15mg -20.9%, placebo -3.1%; >=5% weight loss in 85%/89%/91% vs 35% placebo
trial_detail.regulatory_relationship: pivotal trial supporting FDA approval of Zepbound (tirzepatide) for chronic weight management

thyroid C-cell tumor finding is from rodent studies; human relevance undetermined per the label

is contraindicated in people with a personal or family history of MTC or MEN 2

claims.canonical_claim: Protein intake above the RDA (0.8 g/kg/day) attenuates loss of whole-body lean mass during energy restriction, compared with protein intake at or near the RDA, according to a systematic review and meta-analysis of controlled trials.
claims.support_strength: systematic review and meta-analysis of controlled trials (Tier A)
claims.population: adults undergoing energy restriction (catabolic stress) in the pooled trials
claims.comparator: protein intake at or near the RDA (0.8 g/kg/day)
claims.outcome: attenuation of whole-body lean mass loss
limitations: Effect size and the specific protein intake threshold at which the effect is strongest are not reduced to one number applicable to every individual.
required_qualifiers: applies during energy restriction (catabolic stress); this source does not establish the same effect during energy balance or surplus
prohibited_wording: more protein always builds more muscle regardless of energy balance
the RDA is dangerously insufficient for everyone

claims.canonical_claim: The U.S. National Academies' Adequate Intake for total water is 3.7 liters per day for adult men and 2.7 liters per day for adult women ages 19-30, including water from all beverages and food (approximately 81% from beverages/drinking water and 19% from food).
claims.support_strength: national dietary reference intake report from a government-convened scientific body (Tier A)
claims.population: adult men and women ages 19-30 in the United States
claims.outcome: Adequate Intake (AI) values for total water
limitations: Individual water needs vary with climate, activity level, and health status; this is a population-level reference value, not an individualized target.
required_qualifiers: figure includes water from food, not only from drinking beverages directly
prohibited_wording: everyone must drink exactly this many liters of plain water per day
this is a medical requirement rather than a population reference value

claims.canonical_claim: At six-year follow-up of 14 'Biggest Loser' Season 8 competitors (of 16 originally studied), measured resting metabolic rate (RMR) was on average 704 +/- 427 kcal/day below the same participants' measured baseline (pre-competition) RMR (P<0.0001), despite substantial weight regain in most participants.
claims.support_strength: single long-term (6-year) observational follow-up cohort (Tier A); small sample size
claims.population: 14 of the original 16 'Biggest Loser' Season 8 competitors
claims.outcome: measured six-year resting metabolic rate relative to the same participants' measured baseline RMR (raw comparison of two measured values, not adjusted for 6-year body composition)
limitations: Very small sample size (n=14 of 16 original competitors).
Single reality-TV-derived cohort with an unusually extreme initial weight-loss intervention; may not generalize to typical weight-loss approaches.

This is a raw comparison of two measured RMR values (baseline vs. six-year); it is NOT the same figure as this source's separately defined 'metabolic adaptation' residual (see claim-biggestloser-metabolic-adaptation-residual), which differs materially because it additionally adjusts for the participant's actual body composition and age at the 6-year visit.
confounders: Substantial weight regain occurred in most participants during the follow-up period, which itself interacts with metabolic rate.
required_qualifiers: based on a very small (n=14), atypical cohort; not a general population estimate
this is the raw measured-six-year-vs-measured-baseline RMR difference, not the source's separately defined 'metabolic adaptation' figure
prohibited_wording: proves that weight loss permanently and irreversibly damages metabolism for everyone
applies to typical, moderate weight-loss programs
is the same number as this source's metabolic adaptation figure
baseline-predicted
predicted from baseline

statistical_detail.measure_type: mean difference between measured six-year resting metabolic rate and the same participants' measured baseline resting metabolic rate (unadjusted for 6-year body composition)
statistical_detail.comparison: measured six-year RMR vs measured baseline RMR

claims.notes: Split from the former single claim "claim-adaptive-thermogenesis-rmr-suppression" during the Stage 3 closure pass (Issue #28): that claim's own statistical_detail was correctly the raw -704 figure, but the topic/packet allowed_conclusions that referenced it had used 'metabolic adaptation' language for it — improperly conflating this raw figure with the source's distinctly-defined, smaller-magnitude 'metabolic adaptation' residual. This claim (Claim A) is the raw measured-baseline-vs-measured-six-year RMR difference only. See claim-biggestloser-metabolic-adaptation-residual for Claim B, the source's separately defined 'metabolic adaptation' residual. Independently re-verified against the PubMed abstract: "RMR was 704 +/- 427 kcal/day below baseline (P < 0.0001)" — this comparison is against the participants' own measured baseline RMR, not a predicted value. Corrected during a follow-up Issue #28 review pass: this claim previously described its comparator as a "baseline-predicted value"/"value predicted from... baseline measurements," which incorrectly borrowed the terminology of the source's separate, adjusted 'metabolic adaptation' residual (claim-biggestloser-metabolic-adaptation-residual) — the -704 figure is a comparison of two directly measured RMR values, not a predicted/modeled one.

claims.canonical_claim: In the same 6-year follow-up of 14 'Biggest Loser' Season 8 competitors, the paper's specifically defined 'metabolic adaptation' — the residual resting metabolic rate (RMR) after statistically adjusting for each participant's actual body composition and age at the 6-year visit — was -499 +/- 207 kcal/day (P<0.0001), a smaller-magnitude figure than the raw measured-baseline-vs-measured-six-year RMR difference (see claim-biggestloser-rmr-below-baseline).
claims.support_strength: single long-term (6-year) observational follow-up cohort (Tier A); small sample size
claims.population: 14 of the original 16 'Biggest Loser' Season 8 competitors
claims.outcome: metabolic adaptation, as the paper defines it: residual RMR after adjusting for body composition and age
limitations: Very small sample size (n=14 of 16 original competitors).
Single reality-TV-derived cohort with an unusually extreme initial weight-loss intervention; may not generalize to typical weight-loss approaches.

The adjustment removes the portion of RMR suppression attributable to changed body composition, so this number is not interchangeable with the raw measured-baseline-vs-measured-six-year RMR difference (see claim-biggestloser-rmr-below-baseline).
confounders: Substantial weight regain occurred in most participants during the follow-up period, which itself interacts with body composition and therefore with this adjusted residual.
required_qualifiers: based on a very small (n=14), atypical cohort; not a general population estimate
'metabolic adaptation' here is a specific statistical residual (adjusted for body composition and age), not simply 'how far below baseline RMR remains'
prohibited_wording: proves that weight loss permanently and irreversibly damages metabolism for everyone
applies to typical, moderate weight-loss programs
is the same number as the raw RMR-below-baseline figure
simply how far below baseline RMR remains

statistical_detail.measure_type: metabolic adaptation: residual resting metabolic rate after adjusting for changes in body composition and age (deviation from statistically predicted RMR under that adjustment model)
statistical_detail.comparison: adjusted metabolic-adaptation residual relative to predicted RMR after accounting for body composition and age

claims.notes: Split out during the Stage 3 closure pass (Issue #28) as Claim B alongside claim-biggestloser-rmr-below-baseline (Claim A) — see that claim's notes for why the split was needed. Independently re-verified against the PubMed abstract: "Metabolic adaptation was defined as the residual RMR after adjusting for changes in body composition and age" ... "metabolic adaptation was -499 +/- 207 kcal/day (P < 0.0001)." A follow-up Issue #28 review pass corrected Claim A's comparator wording (it had incorrectly borrowed "baseline-predicted" language that actually describes this claim's adjusted/predicted residual); this claim's own wording was already correct and required no change beyond tightening its cross-references to Claim A.
